newsitem.title: CANADA: Brazil Gov sees Canada, Argentine wheat imports up.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Gov sees Canada, Argentine wheat imports up.

text.p: Brazil will likely increase its imports of Canadian and Argentine wheat due to market liberalizations and growing demand, the governor of Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul said Wednesday.
"We already import a great quantity of grains from Canada, and in the opening of our markets we will increase those imports," Governor Antonio Britto told reporters.

Brazil imported 1.12 million tonnes of wheat from Canada in crop year 1995/96 (Aug/July) and 56,000 tonnes of barley compared to an annual average of 879,000 tonnes of wheat and 9,000 tonnes of barley over the preceding 10 years.

"The food consumption in Brazil has grown around 30 percent in the last three years and we haven't been able to accompany the wheat production at the same pace, this means we intend to give many happy moments to producers from Argentina and Canada," Britto said after signing a memorandum of trade cooperation with Manitoba Premier Gary Filmon.
Canadian exports to Brazil totalled C$912.4 million in calendar 1995 while imports reached C$777 million in value, Manitoba Industry and Trade statistics show.
Manitoba sold C$37.4 million-worth of wheat, barley, vegetables, nickel and insecticides to Brazil in 1995.
The Canadian province bought C$25 million in coffee, leather, plastics and diesel engines from Brazil in 1995.
Britto led a trade mission from his state to Manitoba on Wednesday and Thursday which was expected to sign at least three cooperative ventures including one on beef genetics.
"We already have a good technological standard (in beef genetics) but we are always interested in learning," Britto said.
Manitoba Premier Filmon said he hoped to visit Brazil and Argentina in January if re-elected Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien proceeds with earlier plans for a trade mission.
"This agreement (with Rio Grande do Sul) is significant in that it indicates we're ready to expand our market opportunities in South America in general and Brazil in particular," Filmon said.
